Validating a High-Performance Cloud Object Store with Lightweight Formal Methods
description: Abstract: We report on our experience validating S3 Express One Zone, a high-performance Amazon S3 storage class launched in November 2023. We focused on its distributed metadata index, which implements a hierarchical namespace using distributed transactions. We check strong consistency and durability under crashes, network delays, and timeouts. Building on our prior work on lightweight formal methods, we combined executable reference models with property-based testing and stateless model checking. Applying these techniques to a production distributed system required three new techniques: a white-box approach to checking serializability; compositional validation of the data and control planes; and long-running canaries that use reference models to check correctness across deployments. We extended Shuttle, our open-source stateless checker, to support a production async Rust runtime and failure injection, including cancelled operations and timeouts. Our main finding is that this approach is sustainable at engineering scale. After launch, the engineering team took ownership of models and test infrastructure, increasing its share of validation commits from 41% to 84% and independently extending the models for conditional writes, object append, and atomic rename, with little involvement from the formal methods team.

Morty — Continue your AI agent from any browser
description:
I built a small open-source tool to solve a specific annoyance: being able to keep using the AI agent running on my machine when I’m not sitting in front of it.

Previously I used Tailscale + Moshi. It worked, but the experience was laggy and I had to run my own relay to make it tolerable. Other tools that appeared later were either heavyweight or closed-source — I wasn’t comfortable handing my machine to something I couldn’t inspect.

Morty is intentionally narrow. It lets you continue a Claude Code, Codex, or Pi session from any browser (phone, tablet, another laptop). No account, no app install, no manual config. You paste one prompt into an existing session; the agent fetches a public setup document and does the rest (including installing prerequisites if needed). Then you open the link it gives you (or scan a QR code).

Design choices that mattered to me:

  • Conversation history stays on your machine. The browser only ever reads it live from the local daemon; nothing is stored in the cloud.
  • Session payloads are end-to-end encrypted between the browser and the daemon. The Cloudflare relay only forwards ciphertext.
  • Apache 2.0, free for now (the relay isn’t expensive yet).
  • Explicit, time-limited, revocable sharing links if you ever want someone else to join a session.

Setup prompt (paste into any Claude Code / Codex / Pi session):

Fetch https://morty.build/doc/setup.md and complete the Morty setup for me.
You may install missing prerequisites and pair this machine.

Site: https://morty.build
Repo: https://github.com/portalcrew/morty

It’s still early. Known limitations exist (machine has to stay awake, terminal sessions can fork if you don’t exit them first, etc.). Feedback, issues, and critique are welcome.

Maak v1.0.0 :: infinitely extensible command runner, build sys in Lisp
description:
maak is a command runner, and its task list is a Lisp file. You write maak.scm, a perfectly normal Lisp (Guile Scheme) module, and every procedure in it becomes a task you can name on the command line. There is no DSL to learn and no second language to keep in your head: the build is the program.

Repo: https://github.com/jjba23/maak

(define-module (maak)
  #:declarative? #t
  #:use-module (maak maak))

(define (deploy host)
  "Ship release.tar.gz to HOST."
  (build)
  (run (list "rsync" "-avz" "release.tar.gz"
             (string-append host ":srv/www/"))))


$ maak deploy -- example.org

The docstring is the entry maak --list prints. The lambda list is the argument grammar. Tasks call each other with a function call, not a subprocess that re-parses a file. There is no second language, and nothing to keep in sync between the task list and the code that runs.

  • run takes a program and its arguments as separate strings, so a path with a space in it stays one argument.
  • run-pipeline connects stages with pipe/dup2, reports every failing stage instead of only the last one, can tee what a stage wrote, and can run the whole pipeline as a background job with a pid you can poll.
  • maak -j 4 -- fmt,lint,test forks a worker per task and prints each task's output as one block, in the order you named them.
  • Dry run and quiet are Scheme parameters, so a test can parameterize them instead of threading --dry-run through five layers.
  • A task can declare #:depends, #:hidden? and #:example, and -j orders by those dependencies instead of only fanning out.

You can also use plain static Maak files, maak.yaml, maak.toml and maak.json work with the same --list, --plan and --watch and running of course.

version: 1

tasks:
  lint:
    doc: Lint and format-check, failing on warnings.
    commands:
      - [cargo, clippy, --, -D, warnings]
      - [cargo, fmt, --check]

maak --plan deploy -- example.org runs nothing and prints the typed plan: each argv, working directory, environment, elevation, and whether it would run in the background. With --json the same plan is a versioned object a CI job can archive or diff.

maak explain deploy prints the call graph (what deploy calls, what calls deploy), the load path, the escalation, and which .env file wins for each variable. It answers "why did this run as root" without making you read the file.

There is also maak --watch TASK, which re-runs and reloads the file on change, and maak --list --json, the versioned task description that the Emacs, Neovim, Vim, VS Code, Helix, IntelliJ, Zed and Sublime integrations all read.

Supporting many features for common development and devex, cargo and rustup, uv and pyproject, npm/pnpm/yarn, Maven and Gradle, Guix and Nix (a pinned Guix resolves to a value a task can decide on, not a string another tool re-reads), Podman/Docker and Compose, git, tar and zip, curl and wget, GNU gettext, Emacs Lisp packaging, sift, and Veritas.

I'd love to hear your thoughts, critique and ideas! More improvements to come for sure, now actively looking into improving some shell completions and more things 😄

Happy hacking :)
